feedback.worked_solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=4x(1-5x)-xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-5y+10xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x(1-5x)-xy)=4-40x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x(1-5x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-5y+10xy)=10y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-5y+10xy)=-5+10x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}4-40x-y & -x \\ 10y & -5+10x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0.2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}4-40(0.2)-0 & -0.2 \\ 10(0) & -5+10(0.2)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -0.2 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Since the eigenvalues are real and both negative, our equilibrium is $\text{an asymptotically stable}$ $\text{sink}.$
